Ancient sea and sky monsters: who came f.Cameroceras: This giant cone-shelled nautiloid hunted in Ordovician seas and may have been one of the biggest animals of its time, with a shell several meters long.
Ancient sea and sky monsters: who came f.Eurypterus (sea scorpion): Not a true scorpion, it was an arthropod up to about a meter long in many species, and it is the state fossil of New York.
Ancient sea and sky monsters: who came f.Helicoprion: A shark relative with a spiral whorl of teeth in its lower jaw, a baffling oddity until scans showed how it fit inside.
Ancient sea and sky monsters: who came f.Nothosaurus: This reptile had a long snout of fish-trapping teeth, hunting in shallow Triassic seas, relative of the later plesiosaurs.
Ancient sea and sky monsters: who came f.Shonisaurus: Nevada's state fossil, this giant ichthyosaur reached about 15 meters, found in remote desert mountains.
Ancient sea and sky monsters: who came f.Liopleurodon: A fearsome Jurassic pliosaur whose size was exaggerated on TV, but at maybe 6 to 7 meters it was still a top predator.
Ancient sea and sky monsters: who came f.Pteranodon: This toothless pterosaur had a wingspan of about six meters and a long head crest, and was a flying reptile, not a dinosaur.
Ancient sea and sky monsters: who came f.Mosasaurus: Mosasaurs were giant marine lizards, related to snakes and monitors, and this one was named for the Meuse river in the Netherlands.
Ancient sea and sky monsters: who came f.Basilosaurus: This early whale grew around 18 meters, and was named king lizard by mistake, before anatomists realized it was a mammal.
Ancient sea and sky monsters: who came f.Livyatan: This giant sperm whale with teeth up to 36 cm was found in Peru in 2008, and its species name melvillei honors Moby-Dick author Herman Melville.

Animal astronauts: first flights.Fruit flies: A US team flew them on a captured German V-2 rocket to study radiation, and they were recovered alive.
Animal astronauts: first flights.Albert II, rhesus monkey: Albert II was the first monkey to reach space at about 134 km, but his parachute failed and he died on impact.
Animal astronauts: first flights.Dezik and Tsygan, dogs: They were Soviet dogs plucked from Moscow's streets and were the first to reach space and return alive.
Animal astronauts: first flights.Laika: The Moscow stray orbited on Sputnik 2 and died within hours from heat, a sad fact that the mission was never meant to be survivable.
Animal astronauts: first flights.Ham the chimp: He flew before Alan Shepard, trained to pull levers on cue, and lived about 17 more years at the zoo after his flight.
Animal astronauts: first flights.Félicette the cat: She is the only cat known to have flown in space, a Paris stray sent up by France and recovered safely after a brief flight.
Animal astronauts: first flights.Tortoises (Zond 5): Zond 5 carried them around the Moon and back, making them the first Earthlings to do it, before Apollo 8 astronauts did.
Animal astronauts: first flights.Spiders Anita and Arabella: On Skylab they spun webs in microgravity, first oddly thin and uneven and later close to normal.
Animal astronauts: first flights.Jellyfish (Space Shuttle): These moon jellies flew on the Space Shuttle, and those born in orbit had trouble swimming normally back on Earth.
Animal astronauts: first flights.Tardigrades (exposed to space): These microscopic animals survived the vacuum and radiation of open space, and some even laid eggs that hatched.

Fat content of these dairy products.Skim milk: Fat is skimmed off using a centrifuge, hence the name, and the result is nearly fat-free.
Fat content of these dairy products.Cultured buttermilk: Traditional buttermilk was the liquid left after churning butter, but today's version is cultured and has no butter in it.
Fat content of these dairy products.Whole milk: Homogenization breaks the fat into tiny droplets so cream does not rise to the top.
Fat content of these dairy products.Half-and-half: This North American mix of equal parts milk and cream is a staple for coffee.
Fat content of these dairy products.Sour cream: Cultured with lactic acid bacteria, it is called smetana in Russia and is spooned onto borscht.
Fat content of these dairy products.Whipping cream: It needs roughly 30 percent or more fat to whip, because the fat globules trap air bubbles.
Fat content of these dairy products.Double cream: This British cream is so rich that if you over-whip it, it turns into butter.
Fat content of these dairy products.Clotted cream: Made by slow heating, it forms a golden crust, and Cornish clotted cream has protected status in Europe.
Fat content of these dairy products.Butter: Churning cream until the fat clumps together leaves behind buttermilk, with about 16 percent water in the butter.
Fat content of these dairy products.Ghee: Heating butter and removing the water and milk solids leaves this, which keeps for months without a fridge in India.

When these game consoles first launched.Magnavox Odyssey: The first home console had no sound and used plastic overlays on the screen; its tennis game inspired Atari's Pong.
When these game consoles first launched.Atari 2600: It popularised cartridges and joysticks; its unsold E.T. games were famously buried in a New Mexico landfill.
When these game consoles first launched.Famicom (NES): Japan's red-and-white machine launched in 1983; the redesigned version reached North America in 1985 as the NES.
When these game consoles first launched.Game Boy: Bundled with Tetris, this grey brick had a murky green screen yet ran for many hours on four AA batteries.
When these game consoles first launched.PlayStation: It began as a failed Sony-Nintendo CD add-on partnership; Sony went solo, and the result outsold Nintendo's cartridge machine.
When these game consoles first launched.Nintendo 64: Its controller popularised the analog stick on a major console, and it stuck with cartridges instead of discs.
When these game consoles first launched.PlayStation 2: One of the best-selling consoles ever, at over 150 million units, it also played DVDs.
When these game consoles first launched.Wii: Its motion controls and bundled Wii Sports brought grandparents into gaming; the name was meant to sound like 'we'.
When these game consoles first launched.PlayStation 4: It sold over 100 million units, and its share button made recording and posting clips easy.
When these game consoles first launched.Nintendo Switch: This hybrid docks to a TV or goes handheld, and has sold over 150 million units.

Sneaky longitudes: Americas from west to.Reno: Reno is farther west than Los Angeles, a surprise since California looks westmost; the city's slogan is the Biggest Little City.
Sneaky longitudes: Americas from west to.Los Angeles: Despite being in California, it sits east of Reno, Nevada.
Sneaky longitudes: Americas from west to.San Diego: California's coast bends southeast, so this city is farther east than LA.
Sneaky longitudes: Americas from west to.Atlanta: Though in the east, it is farther west than Detroit and Miami, which surprises many.
Sneaky longitudes: Americas from west to.Detroit: Canada lies south of it; it is the only major US city with Canada to its south, across the river in Windsor.
Sneaky longitudes: Americas from west to.Miami: It lies west of New York, a surprise, since Florida looks east of the Northeast.
Sneaky longitudes: Americas from west to.Panama City: The canal runs northwest to southeast, so the Pacific end lies east of the Atlantic end.
Sneaky longitudes: Americas from west to.Lima: It sits on nearly the same meridian as Washington, DC, even though one is in South America.
Sneaky longitudes: Americas from west to.New York: The 74th meridian west runs through New York and down through Colombia, near Bogota.
Sneaky longitudes: Americas from west to.Santiago, Chile: Though Chile is on South America's west coast, this capital lies east of New York.

Mammal milestones: who came first?.Morganucodon: Shrew-sized and probably nocturnal, it lived alongside early dinosaurs.
Mammal milestones: who came first?.Juramaia: Found in China, this fossil is the earliest known eutherian, an ancestor of placental mammals.
Mammal milestones: who came first?.Repenomamus: This badger-sized Chinese mammal fossil had baby dinosaur bones in its stomach.
Mammal milestones: who came first?.Purgatorius: A tiny tree-dwelling creature from just after the dinosaurs died out, thought to be an early primate relative.
Mammal milestones: who came first?.Eohippus: Also called Hyracotherium, it was a fox-sized ancestor of the horse with four toes in front.
Mammal milestones: who came first?.Paraceratherium: A hornless rhino relative that browsed treetops like a giraffe, among the largest land mammals ever.
Mammal milestones: who came first?.Proconsul: An early ape from East Africa that walked on all fours and had no tail.
Mammal milestones: who came first?.Deinotherium: An elephant relative with downward-curving tusks on its lower jaw.
Mammal milestones: who came first?.Smilodon: The saber-toothed tiger was no tiger, and its canines were up to 18 cm.
Mammal milestones: who came first?.Woolly rhino: An Ice Age giant with two horns, the front one over a metre long, hunted by early humans.

Binary numbers by value.11: With only 0 and 1 as digits, it's the language computers use, because circuits are either on or off.
Binary numbers by value.101: Leibniz promoted the system in 1703, and saw 1 and 0 as a symbol of creation from nothing.
Binary numbers by value.111: All three bits are on, and in Unix file permissions, the digit 7 means read, write and execute together.
Binary numbers by value.1001: Four bits make a nibble, which counts from 0 to 15.
Binary numbers by value.1100: In hexadecimal, it is simply the letter C.
Binary numbers by value.10000: Hexadecimal is popular with programmers because each hex digit stands for exactly four binary digits.
Binary numbers by value.10101: Its alternating pattern makes it a handy test pattern, since every neighbouring bit differs.
Binary numbers by value.11111: It's one less than 2 to the 5th power, and a Mersenne prime.
Binary numbers by value.100000: A power of two, 2 to the 5th, and 32-bit systems can address about four gigabytes of memory.
Binary numbers by value.1100100: It takes seven bits to write, while a single byte can count up to 255.

When these bizarre episodes happened.Diogenes snubs Alexander: Asked what he wanted by Alexander the Great, the philosopher reportedly said to stand out of his sunlight.
When these bizarre episodes happened.Caligula's war on seashells: The historian Suetonius claims the emperor ordered his soldiers to gather seashells as spoils of the sea.
When these bizarre episodes happened.Simeon climbs his pillar: This Syrian monk spent decades atop a pillar, drawing crowds of pilgrims for advice.
When these bizarre episodes happened.Sky ship seen at Clonmacnoise: The Irish annals say a ship sailed through the air over the congregation, and its anchor caught on the church door.
When these bizarre episodes happened.Pope tried as a corpse: Pope Stephen VI had his predecessor Formosus dug up and put on trial in the Cadaver Synod.
When these bizarre episodes happened.Pied Piper leads children off: The story from Hamelin, Germany, says 130 children were led away; the oldest record dates from around this time.
When these bizarre episodes happened.Flagellants sweep Europe: During the Black Death, groups whipped themselves in public as penance, and Pope Clement VI condemned the movement.
When these bizarre episodes happened.Dancing plague in Aachen: Hundreds danced uncontrollably in the streets; the 1518 episode in Strasbourg is better known.
When these bizarre episodes happened.Pig hanged for murder, Falaise: A sow dressed in human clothes was tried and executed for killing a baby, and such animal trials were once real.
When these bizarre episodes happened.Bal des Ardents fire: King Charles VI of France survived when costumes caught fire at a masked ball; four dancers died.

Whose face is on which US banknote.George Washington: The $1 bill is the most printed US note, with a typical life of around six years, and carries the Great Seal on its back.
Whose face is on which US banknote.Thomas Jefferson: This note is still printed, but rare in circulation, so many people hoard it as a curiosity.
Whose face is on which US banknote.Abraham Lincoln: The Lincoln Memorial appears on the back of this note, echoing the penny's Lincoln.
Whose face is on which US banknote.Alexander Hamilton: The first Treasury Secretary is one of only two non-presidents on current US notes, alongside Franklin.
Whose face is on which US banknote.Andrew Jackson: Andrew Jackson opposed paper money and national banks, which makes his place on a banknote ironic.
Whose face is on which US banknote.Ulysses S. Grant: He led Union armies to victory in the Civil War before serving two terms as president from 1869.
Whose face is on which US banknote.Benjamin Franklin: Franklin was never president, yet he is on the $100, whose blue 3D security ribbon is high-tech.
Whose face is on which US banknote.William McKinley: The $500 bill was last printed in 1945, and large notes were discontinued in 1969.
Whose face is on which US banknote.Grover Cleveland: Grover Cleveland served two nonconsecutive terms as the 22nd and 24th president, and the $1,000 note is long retired.
Whose face is on which US banknote.James Madison: This note is so rare that surviving examples sell to collectors for far more than their face value.

Clothing inventions, oldest to newest.Mackintosh raincoat: Charles Macintosh patented waterproof cloth sandwiching rubber between fabrics, and his name became British slang for any raincoat.
Clothing inventions, oldest to newest.Bowler hat: Lock & Co. made this hard hat for the Norfolk landowner William Coke, so his gamekeepers' heads were protected from low branches, before city gents adopted it.
Clothing inventions, oldest to newest.Riveted blue jeans: Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented copper rivets to reinforce pocket corners, and the first pair were made for miners and workers.
Clothing inventions, oldest to newest.Converse All Star: It began as a basketball shoe, and the player Chuck Taylor became its famous ambassador, so his signature sits on the ankle patch.
Clothing inventions, oldest to newest.Nylon stockings: DuPont unveiled nylon as the 'miracle fiber' and its first stockings sold out in hours in 1940, as women queued to buy them.
Clothing inventions, oldest to newest.Bikini: Named for Bikini Atoll after nuclear tests, the swimsuit was introduced by French designer Louis Réard, who said it was the world's smallest.
Clothing inventions, oldest to newest.Spandex: DuPont chemist Joseph Shivers created it, and the word is an anagram of 'expands'; it is known as Lycra in some markets.
Clothing inventions, oldest to newest.Gore-Tex: The waterproof, breathable fabric is made by stretching PTFE, the same plastic as Teflon, into a membrane with billions of tiny pores.
Clothing inventions, oldest to newest.Polar fleece: Malden Mills invented it and, famously, chose not to patent it; Patagonia popularized it and later made some from recycled plastic bottles.
Clothing inventions, oldest to newest.Crocs: These foam clogs from Colorado were first designed as boat shoes, and their holes were meant to drain water from decks.

Everyday waves by wavelength.Germicidal UV lamp: Germicidal lamps emit UV-C light that damages microbes' DNA, and it can burn human skin and eyes, so such lamps are never used with people nearby.
Everyday waves by wavelength.Blacklight: Blacklights make fluorescent materials glow, and they help reveal hidden security marks on banknotes and some stamps.
Everyday waves by wavelength.Blue LED: Blue LEDs were the last piece of the puzzle needed for white LED lighting, and their inventors won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Everyday waves by wavelength.Green laser pointer: Green laser pointers appear much brighter than red ones of the same power because the human eye is most sensitive to green light.
Everyday waves by wavelength.Sodium streetlight: The orange glow of the old low-pressure sodium lamps is almost a single color, which means that astronomers loved it as easy to filter out.
Everyday waves by wavelength.Red laser pointer: Red laser pointers are the most common, and they typically use a semiconductor diode, as in a DVD player.
Everyday waves by wavelength.TV remote (infrared): Remote controls flicker at about 940 nm, which is invisible to us but visible to a phone camera, so you can see the beam on your screen.
Everyday waves by wavelength.Car radar (77 GHz): Cars' driving-assist radars use a band around 77 GHz, which allows tiny antennas, and it gauges the distance and speed of vehicles ahead.
Everyday waves by wavelength.2.4 GHz Wi-Fi: Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz shares its frequency with microwave ovens, so a running oven can disrupt the signal.
Everyday waves by wavelength.BBC longwave radio: Longwave radio's very long wavelength lets signals follow the ground's curve, and the UK's Droitwich transmitter has been broadcasting since 1934.

Tim Burton films by release.Pee-wee's Big Adventure: Pee-wee's Big Adventure was Burton's feature debut, a comedy about a man in search of his stolen bicycle, with a first score by Danny Elfman.
Tim Burton films by release.Beetlejuice: Beetlejuice was made for a modest budget and became a hit, and Michael Keaton's ghost spends only about 17 minutes onscreen.
Tim Burton films by release.Batman: Batman's dark, gothic Gotham changed superhero movies and brought both Keaton as the hero and Jack Nicholson's Joker to a huge audience.
Tim Burton films by release.Edward Scissorhands: Burton came up with the character of Edward from a childhood drawing, and Johnny Depp's first of many collaborations with him had very few lines of dialogue.
Tim Burton films by release.Ed Wood: Ed Wood was shot in black and white and tells the story of a filmmaker often dubbed the worst ever, with Martin Landau winning an Oscar as Bela Lugosi.
Tim Burton films by release.Mars Attacks!: Mars Attacks! parodies 1950s B-movie alien invasions and was inspired by a series of trading cards, with Slim Whitman's yodeling defeating the invaders.
Tim Burton films by release.Sleepy Hollow: Sleepy Hollow reimagined Washington Irving's legend as a horror mystery, and its sets were built in the English countryside rather than New York.
Tim Burton films by release.Planet of the Apes (Burton): Planet of the Apes was Burton's remake of the 1968 classic, and its twist ending is among his most baffling and debated.
Tim Burton films by release.Big Fish: Big Fish follows a storyteller whose tall tales may or may not be true, and was adapted into a stage musical in 2013.
Tim Burton films by release.Sweeney Todd: Sweeney Todd, adapted from Sondheim's musical, features Depp and Helena Bonham Carter singing and won an Oscar for its art direction.

Turning points in German history.Luther's 95 Theses: It is traditionally said to have been nailed to the Wittenberg church door, though historians debate that, and the printing press spread it widely.
Turning points in German history.German Peasants' War: It was the largest popular uprising in Europe before the French Revolution, and Luther condemned the rebels.
Turning points in German history.Frederick the Great crowned: He played the flute and composed music, and promoted the potato across Prussia to fight hunger.
Turning points in German history.Battle of Leipzig: Called the Battle of the Nations, it was Europe's biggest battle before World War I, and ended Napoleon's hold on Germany.
Turning points in German history.Frankfurt Parliament: It was the first freely elected all-German parliament, but the Prussian king rejected the crown it offered.
Turning points in German history.Germany unified: The empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, after victory over France.
Turning points in German history.Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicates: He fled to the Netherlands and lived at Doorn until his death in 1941.
Turning points in German history.Hitler becomes chancellor: President Hindenburg appointed him on 30 January 1933, rather than voters electing him outright.
Turning points in German history.Berlin Wall built: It went up overnight on 13 August 1961 and stood for 28 years.
Turning points in German history.Reunification: The date, 3 October, is now Germany's national holiday, the Day of German Unity.

Marvel heroes, by first comic appearance.Captain America: He debuted on a cover in 1941 punching Hitler, almost a year before the US entered the war.
Marvel heroes, by first comic appearance.The Fantastic Four: Their debut launched the Marvel Age of comics, created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby.
Marvel heroes, by first comic appearance.Spider-Man: He debuted in Amazing Fantasy #15, as a teen hero rather than a sidekick.
Marvel heroes, by first comic appearance.Iron Man: Tony Stark was created in the Cold War as an arms industrialist, appearing in Tales of Suspense #39.
Marvel heroes, by first comic appearance.Daredevil: Lawyer Matt Murdock is blind, but his other senses are heightened.
Marvel heroes, by first comic appearance.Black Panther: He was the first Black superhero in mainstream American comics, ruling the nation of Wakanda.
Marvel heroes, by first comic appearance.Ghost Rider (Johnny Blaze): Johnny Blaze is a motorcycle stuntman who made a deal with the devil.
Marvel heroes, by first comic appearance.Wolverine: He first appeared as a cameo in The Incredible Hulk #180, as a villain.
Marvel heroes, by first comic appearance.Deadpool: Rob Liefeld and Fabian Nicieza created him in New Mutants #98, known for breaking the fourth wall.
Marvel heroes, by first comic appearance.Miles Morales: Introduced in 2011 in Ultimate Comics, he became the star of Into the Spider-Verse.

Landmark mobile phones by release.Motorola DynaTAC 8000X: Nicknamed 'the brick', it weighed nearly a kilogram and offered about half an hour of talk time after a ten-hour charge.
Landmark mobile phones by release.IBM Simon: Often called the first smartphone, it had a touchscreen, email, fax and a calendar.
Landmark mobile phones by release.BlackBerry 5810: The first BlackBerry phone had no built-in speaker or microphone, so you needed a headset to make calls.
Landmark mobile phones by release.Motorola Razr V3: This ultra-thin flip phone sold over 100 million units, one of the best-selling phones of its era.
Landmark mobile phones by release.Original iPhone: Steve Jobs unveiled it in January 2007, and it had no App Store at launch; apps arrived the following year.
Landmark mobile phones by release.HTC Dream (first Android): Sold as the T-Mobile G1 in the US, it had a slide-out keyboard and a trackball.
Landmark mobile phones by release.Samsung Galaxy S: This launched the Galaxy line that became the biggest Android rival to the iPhone.
Landmark mobile phones by release.Samsung Galaxy Note: Its 5.3-inch screen was mocked as a 'phablet', but huge phones soon became the norm.
Landmark mobile phones by release.Google Pixel: Google's first phone it designed itself, it replaced the Nexus line and made the camera its main selling point.
Landmark mobile phones by release.Samsung Galaxy Fold: Reviewers' early units broke within days, so the release was delayed from April to September.

Scratch test: Mohs hardness.Talc: So soft that a fingernail scratches it; ground up, it is the main ingredient of talcum powder.
Scratch test: Mohs hardness.Gypsum: A fingernail can scratch it; it is used in plasterboard, and a cave in Naica, Mexico, held gypsum crystals up to about 11 metres long.
Scratch test: Mohs hardness.Your fingernail: Geologists often carry a fingernail as a quick test tool, since it scratches gypsum but not calcite.
Scratch test: Mohs hardness.Calcite: The main mineral of limestone and marble; clear Iceland spar crystals split light into a double image.
Scratch test: Mohs hardness.Fluorite: It gave fluorescence its name, because many samples glow under ultraviolet light; its own name comes from the Latin for 'to flow'.
Scratch test: Mohs hardness.Window glass: Dust and sand contain quartz, which outranks glass, and that is why windows and screens get scratched by grit.
Scratch test: Mohs hardness.Quartz: One of the most common minerals in Earth's crust and the main grain of sand; amethyst and citrine are coloured varieties of it.
Scratch test: Mohs hardness.Topaz: Pure topaz is colourless; the golden and pink stones prized in jewellery owe their colour to trace impurities and crystal defects.
Scratch test: Mohs hardness.Corundum (ruby): Ruby is red corundum coloured by chromium, while blue sapphire is the same mineral tinted by iron and titanium.
Scratch test: Mohs hardness.Diamond: Hard is not the same as tough: a sharp blow can cleave a diamond along its crystal planes, which is how cutters shape them.

When these bizarre thefts happened.The Mona Lisa: Louvre worker Vincenzo Peruggia hid it in his flat for two years, and the publicity made the painting the world's most famous.
When these bizarre thefts happened.The Stone of Scone: Four Scottish students took the coronation stone from Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1950, and it broke in two during the grab.
When these bizarre thefts happened.Einstein's brain: Pathologist Thomas Harvey kept it after the autopsy without family permission, cut it into slices and sent pieces to researchers.
When these bizarre thefts happened.The Jules Rimet Trophy: The trophy vanished before the 1966 World Cup and was found a week later under a hedge by a dog called Pickles.
When these bizarre thefts happened.Charlie Chaplin's coffin: Thieves dug up the comedian's coffin in Switzerland and asked for ransom from his widow; it was found buried in a cornfield.
When these bizarre thefts happened.Gardner Museum heist: Two men in police uniforms took 13 works worth around 500 million dollars, including a Vermeer, and the case is still unsolved.
When these bizarre thefts happened.The Scream (Oslo): It was taken from Oslo's National Gallery on the day the Winter Olympics opened in nearby Lillehammer, and was recovered months later.
When these bizarre thefts happened.Great Maple Syrup Heist: Thieves siphoned thousands of tonnes from Quebec's strategic reserve, which acts like an oil reserve for the global supply of syrup.
When these bizarre thefts happened.A truckload of Nutella: A truck carrying around five tonnes of the hazelnut spread was stolen in Germany, and it was worth tens of thousands of euros.
When these bizarre thefts happened.A solid gold toilet: A working 18-carat gold toilet by artist Maurizio Cattelan vanished from Blenheim Palace, the birthplace of Winston Churchill.

When these medieval battles were fought.Catalaunian Plains: Roman general Aetius, with Visigoth allies, stopped Attila the Hun in Gaul; the Visigoth king Theodoric I was killed in the fighting.
When these medieval battles were fought.Talas: Tang China fought the Abbasid Caliphate in Central Asia; tradition says captured Chinese papermakers helped spread papermaking westward.
When these medieval battles were fought.Lechfeld: Otto I crushed the Magyar raiders near Augsburg, ending their attacks on Western Europe; he was crowned emperor in 962.
When these medieval battles were fought.Clontarf: Fought near Dublin, Brian Boru's army beat Viking-allied rivals, but the aged High King was killed in his tent.
When these medieval battles were fought.Las Navas de Tolosa: Christian Iberian kingdoms united against the Almohad caliphate and won a turning point in the Reconquista.
When these medieval battles were fought.Ain Jalut: Near Galilee, the Mamluks defeated a Mongol force and halted the Mongol advance toward Egypt, a rare Mongol loss.
When these medieval battles were fought.Bannockburn: Robert the Bruce's Scots beat a much larger English army near Stirling; England finally recognized Scottish independence in 1328.
When these medieval battles were fought.Kosovo: The Ottomans met a Serbian-led coalition, and both Sultan Murad I and Prince Lazar died; the battle became central to Serbian memory.
When these medieval battles were fought.Grunwald: Poland-Lithuania crushed the Teutonic Knights in one of medieval Europe's largest battles; Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen died on the field.
When these medieval battles were fought.Varna: A crusade led by young King Władysław III of Poland and Hungary was defeated by Sultan Murad II, and the king died in the battle.

Paper and card sizes, by area.A8 sheet: A-series sizes halve neatly, so an A8 sheet is exactly 1/256 of an A0 sheet's one square meter.
Paper and card sizes, by area.US business card: In Japan the exchange of these cards, called meishi, is a ritual involving a two-handed presentation.
Paper and card sizes, by area.Standard US index card: Vladimir Nabokov drafted his novels on these cards, shuffling them to arrange scenes.
Paper and card sizes, by area.A6 sheet: It's postcard-sized, and every ISO paper size keeps the same ratio, the square root of two, when halved.
Paper and card sizes, by area.A5 sheet: A common notebook size, and two A5 pages side by side make an A4 spread.
Paper and card sizes, by area.US Letter: Used in the US, Canada and parts of Latin America, while the rest of the world follows ISO's A4.
Paper and card sizes, by area.A4 sheet: Standard everywhere outside North America, its ratio traces to Georg Lichtenberg's 1786 insight.
Paper and card sizes, by area.US Legal: Named for legal paperwork like contracts, the tall format is rarer now that most documents go digital.
Paper and card sizes, by area.A3 sheet: Twice an A4 sheet, it is common for posters and drawings and folds once to make A4.
Paper and card sizes, by area.A2 sheet: Four times the area of A4, it's used for posters and drawings, and A0 is a full square meter.

When these chess champions first took th.Wilhelm Steinitz: The first official world champion, he pioneered positional play, and argued that attacks only succeed if your position is sound.
When these chess champions first took th.Emanuel Lasker: He held the title for 27 years, longer than anyone, and was also a gifted mathematician, whose name is attached to a theorem in algebra.
When these chess champions first took th.José Raúl Capablanca: The Cuban prodigy reportedly learned the game at four by watching his father, and was admired for his effortless, flawless endgames.
When these chess champions first took th.Alexander Alekhine: He's the only champion to die while still holding the title, in 1946.
When these chess champions first took th.Mikhail Botvinnik: The first Soviet champion was an electrical engineer, and later spent years trying to program a computer to play chess.
When these chess champions first took th.Bobby Fischer: His 1972 match against Boris Spassky in Reykjavik became a Cold War spectacle and a worldwide television event.
When these chess champions first took th.Anatoly Karpov: He became champion in 1975 without playing, when Fischer refused to defend his title.
When these chess champions first took th.Garry Kasparov: In 1985 he became the youngest champion to that point, at 22, and later lost a famous 1997 match to IBM's Deep Blue.
When these chess champions first took th.Magnus Carlsen: The Norwegian became a grandmaster at 13, and held the title for a decade before choosing not to defend it in 2023.
When these chess champions first took th.Gukesh Dommaraju: At 18, he became the youngest undisputed world champion in history, beating China's Ding Liren.

Merriam-Webster Words of the Year, in or.Blog: The word comes from blog, short for weblog, a term coined by Jorn Barger in 1997.
Merriam-Webster Words of the Year, in or.Truthiness: Stephen Colbert coined it on the first episode of The Colbert Report in 2005, to mean what feels true rather than what is.
Merriam-Webster Words of the Year, in or.W00t: A gamer cheer written with zeros in place of the letter o, it was the first Word of the Year to include numerals.
Merriam-Webster Words of the Year, in or.Bailout: Probably from the idea of bailing water out of a sinking boat, it became the word for the 2008 financial crisis rescue.
Merriam-Webster Words of the Year, in or.Austerity: From the Greek austeros, meaning harsh or dry, it described budget cuts imposed during the European debt crisis.
Merriam-Webster Words of the Year, in or.Surreal: Apollinaire coined the French original in 1917 and lookups spiked after the Brexit vote and the 2016 US election.
Merriam-Webster Words of the Year, in or.Feminism: Searches jumped after the Women's March in 2017, though the French word for the movement dates back to the 1800s.
Merriam-Webster Words of the Year, in or.They: Singular they has been in use since at least the 14th century, and in 2019 the dictionary added a nonbinary sense.
Merriam-Webster Words of the Year, in or.Pandemic: From the Greek pan, all, and demos, people, it was looked up far more in 2020 than any other word.
Merriam-Webster Words of the Year, in or.Gaslighting: It comes from the 1938 play Gas Light, later filmed in 1944 with Ingrid Bergman, in which a husband manipulates his wife.

How old these board games are.Senet: A board found in Tutankhamun's tomb; its rules were lost, so modern versions are educated reconstructions.
How old these board games are.Royal Game of Ur: Found in royal graves at Ur, its rules were recovered from a cuneiform tablet written around 177 BC.
How old these board games are.Go: Traced to ancient China, Go has more possible positions than there are atoms in the observable universe.
How old these board games are.Chaturanga: This Indian war game of infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots is the ancestor of both chess and shatranj.
How old these board games are.Chess with the modern queen: Around 1475, in Spain, the queen and bishop gained long-range powers, speeding up play; it was nicknamed 'mad queen chess'.
How old these board games are.Mahjong: Its modern form emerged in China in the 19th century, then became a huge craze in 1920s America.
How old these board games are.The Landlord's Game: Lizzie Magie designed it to show how landlords profit from rents; it was later reworked into Monopoly.
How old these board games are.Scrabble (as Criss-Crosswords): Architect Alfred Butts invented it during the Depression; it was renamed Scrabble in 1948 after James Brunot bought the rights.
How old these board games are.Trivial Pursuit: Created by two Canadian journalists, it began as a game they made after finding a Scrabble set missing pieces.
How old these board games are.Catan: Klaus Teuber's German design helped spark the modern board-game boom, and it has sold tens of millions of copies.

When these mammals were lost forever.Steller's sea cow: This giant kelp-eater, up to 8–9 m long, vanished within about 27 years of European discovery.
When these mammals were lost forever.Bluebuck: This antelope of South Africa is considered the first large African mammal to go extinct in historic times.
When these mammals were lost forever.Atlas bear: Africa's only native bear lived in the Atlas Mountains and was caught for Roman arena shows.
When these mammals were lost forever.Falkland Islands wolf: The warrah was the Falklands' only native land mammal; Darwin predicted its extinction after visiting.
When these mammals were lost forever.Quagga: This zebra relative was striped only on its front, and the last captive died in Amsterdam; breeding projects aim to recreate it.
When these mammals were lost forever.Toolache wallaby: Hunted for sport and fur, this graceful, fast wallaby of South Australia was gone within decades.
When these mammals were lost forever.Caribbean monk seal: The only seal native to the Caribbean, it was declared extinct in 2008.
When these mammals were lost forever.Baiji (Yangtze dolphin): A survey in 2006 failed to find any of these freshwater dolphins, perhaps the first dolphin driven extinct by humans.
When these mammals were lost forever.Western black rhino: This rhino subspecies was declared extinct by the IUCN in 2011, after poaching for its horn.
When these mammals were lost forever.Bramble Cay melomys: Living on a low Great Barrier Reef island that flooded, it may be the first mammal extinction blamed on human-caused climate change.

When women won the national vote.New Zealand: It was the first self-governing country to let all adult women vote, but they could not stand for parliament until 1919.
When women won the national vote.Finland: Then part of the Russian empire, it was the first European nation to enact women's suffrage, and elected 19 women in 1907.
When women won the national vote.Norway: Women gained full voting rights in 1913, after limited rights in 1907.
When women won the national vote.United States: The 19th Amendment was ratified in August 1920, though many Black women were blocked in practice until 1965.
When women won the national vote.Brazil: Women won the vote under Getúlio Vargas's 1932 electoral code.
When women won the national vote.France: De Gaulle's provisional government decreed it in 1944, and women first voted in 1945, late for such a country.
When women won the national vote.Japan: It came under Allied occupation, and 39 women were elected to the Diet in 1946.
When women won the national vote.Mexico: The right was amended into law in 1953, and women voted nationally in 1955.
When women won the national vote.Switzerland: Men voted for it in 1971, and Appenzell Innerrhoden held out until a federal court forced it in 1990.
When women won the national vote.Kuwait: Women gained the vote and the right to run for office in 2005, and the first women ministers followed.

Great firsts in the history of flight.Balloon crosses the Channel: Jean-Pierre Blanchard and American John Jeffries threw out ballast and even clothing to stay aloft before reaching France.
Great firsts in the history of flight.Wright brothers' first flight: The first flight lasted 12 seconds at Kitty Hawk; the best of the brothers' four flights that day reached 59 seconds.
Great firsts in the history of flight.Blériot flies the Channel: He won the Daily Mail's £1,000 prize, crossing in his small monoplane in under 40 minutes.
Great firsts in the history of flight.Alcock and Brown nonstop: Their modified Vickers Vimy bomber flew Newfoundland to Ireland in about 16 hours, landing in a bog; both were knighted.
Great firsts in the history of flight.Lindbergh solo to Paris: His Spirit of St. Louis flight took about 33 hours and won the $25,000 Orteig Prize.
Great firsts in the history of flight.Earhart's solo Atlantic: She was the first woman to cross the Atlantic solo, landing in a Northern Ireland pasture after about 15 hours aloft.
Great firsts in the history of flight.Hindenburg disaster: The German airship burst into flames while landing in New Jersey; 36 people died, and the radio report made the disaster famous.
Great firsts in the history of flight.Yeager breaks sound barrier: Flying a rocket-powered Bell X-1 he had named after his wife, he did it despite broken ribs from a horse accident days earlier.
Great firsts in the history of flight.Comet starts jet service: This de Havilland jetliner began the first jet passenger service with BOAC, but metal fatigue near its square windows caused crashes in 1954.
Great firsts in the history of flight.Concorde enters service: Concorde crossed the Atlantic in under three and a half hours at twice the speed of sound, until retiring in 2003.

Old British money, in pre-1971 pennies.Farthing: A farthing was a quarter of a penny and ended in 1960. Its coins showed a tiny wren, the smallest British bird.
Old British money, in pre-1971 pennies.Penny: The old penny was abbreviated d, from the Roman denarius. 240 of them made one pound before decimalisation.
Old British money, in pre-1971 pennies.Groat: The groat was a silver coin worth fourpence, and its name comes from a word meaning "thick." It was first struck in the 1200s.
Old British money, in pre-1971 pennies.Tanner: Tanner is slang for a sixpence, and nobody is sure why. The silver coin was a staple of pocket money for centuries.
Old British money, in pre-1971 pennies.Shilling (bob): Bob is the slang for a shilling, which stayed the same. It was worth twelve pennies, and 20 of them made a pound.
Old British money, in pre-1971 pennies.Florin: The florin was introduced in 1849 as a step towards decimal money. It lived on as the 10p coin after 1971.
Old British money, in pre-1971 pennies.Half crown: Half a crown was one of Britain's best-known coins, worth two shillings and sixpence. Eight of them made a pound.
Old British money, in pre-1971 pennies.Crown: The crown, worth five shillings, was a large silver coin. Later ones were mostly struck to mark special occasions.
Old British money, in pre-1971 pennies.Sovereign: The gold sovereign was first minted in 1489 under Henry VII. It is still struck today, mostly for collectors and investors.
Old British money, in pre-1971 pennies.Guinea: The guinea was named for the African region where the gold came from. It ended as a coin, but horse races and art auctions still use it.

Toilet milestones through history.Skara Brae drains: On Orkney, this Stone Age village has stone huts with built-in drains that seem to run from a recess in the wall that served as a toilet.
Toilet milestones through history.Minoan palace flush: At Knossos on Crete, a palace had a toilet seat with water flushing it away, more than 3,500 years ago.
Toilet milestones through history.Rome's Cloaca Maxima: Rome's great drain still carries water today; Romans often shared public latrines, wiping with a communal sponge on a stick.
Toilet milestones through history.Harington's flush toilet: Sir John Harington, godson of Elizabeth I, built one for the queen and wrote a book about it, punning on the slang word jakes by calling it Ajax.
Toilet milestones through history.Cumming's S-trap patent: Alexander Cumming's S-shaped bend traps water to block sewer smells, and the same principle sits beneath nearly every toilet today.
Toilet milestones through history.Bramah's improved patent: Joseph Bramah's valve design was so reliable that it stayed in production for decades; he also invented a famously unpickable lock.
Toilet milestones through history.Great Exhibition pay toilets: At the Crystal Palace, visitors paid a penny to use George Jennings's flush toilets, which gave us the phrase to spend a penny.
Toilet milestones through history.Gayetty's toilet paper: Joseph Gayetty's medicated paper was sold in flat packs in New York, with his name watermarked on every sheet.
Toilet milestones through history.TOTO Washlet: Japan's TOTO launched the seat with a warm-water spray, and it became so common in Japanese homes that it is now a standard fixture.
Toilet milestones through history.UN World Toilet Day: The UN made November 19 official to draw attention to the billions of people who still lack access to safe sanitation.

Louis Braille and Braille.Louis Braille born: Born in Coupvray near Paris, the son of a harness maker, Louis grew up around the very awls and tools that would change his life.
Louis Braille and Braille.Braille blinded: Louis was blinded after injuring his eye with a tool in his father's workshop, and infection spread to both eyes by about age five.
Louis Braille and Braille.Braille devises his system: At just 15, Braille adapted a night-writing code of raised dots from army captain Charles Barbier, shrinking it to a six-dot cell.
Louis Braille and Braille.First Braille book: Braille published the first book explaining his system, using it to teach the method to others, including how to write music notation.
Louis Braille and Braille.Braille dies: He died of tuberculosis at 43, long before his system was widely accepted, after years as a respected teacher at the school he once attended.
Louis Braille and Braille.France adopts Braille: Two years after his death, the Institute for Blind Youth in Paris officially adopted his system, which had long been used by the students.
Louis Braille and Braille.Standard English Braille: Agreement on one English Braille code came after years of rival tactile systems, which had forced blind readers to learn several of them.
Louis Braille and Braille.Perkins Brailler: Made at the Perkins School for the Blind, this six-key machine let blind writers punch Braille quickly, and it remained a classroom staple for decades.
Louis Braille and Braille.Braille moved to the Panthéon: On the centenary of his death, France moved Braille's remains to the Panthéon, though his hands were kept in his home village.
Louis Braille and Braille.First World Braille Day: The UN chose January 4, Braille's birthday, for this annual day promoting access to information and rights for blind and partially sighted people.
